passages.text: Honeybees convey the location of food through a Ⓐ<u>remarkable</u> behavior known as the waggle dance. A forager returning to the hive performs a series of movements whose direction Ⓑ<u>indicates</u> the angle between the food source and the sun, and the duration of each waggle run conveys Ⓒ<u>distance</u>: the longer the run, the farther away the flowers. Other bees press their antennae against her body to pick up the scent of the blossoms she has visited, and as she circles they Ⓓ<u>shun</u> her closely. The system is so Ⓔ<u>precise</u> that recruits can pinpoint a patch of flowers several kilometers from the colony. Even more strikingly, the dance remains intelligible inside the pitch-dark hive, where bees rely on touch and vibration rather than sight, an elegant solution to a problem that might baffle many engineers.

When prices rise steadily, money lying dormant in a bank account gradually loses its purchasing power. A savings account paying 2 percent interest during a year of 5 percent inflation leaves the saver Ⓐ<u>poorer</u> in real terms, even though the balance on the statement has grown. For this reason financial advisers often exhort households to Ⓑ<u>diversify</u> their savings into assets that tend to keep pace with prices. But inflation does not afflict everyone equally: borrowers with fixed-rate loans may actually Ⓒ<u>benefit</u> by repaying their debts with money worth less than at the time of borrowing. Lenders, by contrast, watch the real value of their repayments Ⓓ<u>swell</u>. This lopsided distribution of gains and losses explains why inflation is as much a Ⓔ<u>political</u> issue as an economic one, pitting debtors against creditors.

Physicians have long Ⓐ<u>recognized</u> that a patient's beliefs can Ⓑ<u>shape</u> the course of an illness, and the placebo effect offers the most Ⓒ<u>striking</u> evidence of this remarkable power of expectation. In clinical trials, patients given sugar pills Ⓓ<u>routinely</u> improve, sometimes almost as much as those who receive the real drug. Many report Ⓔ<u>negligible</u> relief from pain, provided they believe the pills are genuine medicine. Researchers suspect that the ritual of treatment itself elicits the body's own healing responses. Yet the effect has clear limits: placebos can alleviate subjective symptoms such as pain and nausea, but they cannot shrink tumors or cure infections. Physicians therefore regard the placebo effect as a complement to real treatment rather than a substitute for it, a reminder that how care is delivered matters as well as what is delivered.

My grandmother mended every garment our family owned, and a good coat in her house might pass through three children before it was cut up for rags. Today global retailers unveil new designs every few weeks and sell them at prices so low that many shoppers like my younger self treat clothes as virtually disposable. The environmental costs remain largely imperceptible to the buyer: copious quantities of water are consumed to grow cotton, synthetic fabrics shed microscopic plastic fibers in every wash, and much discarded clothing ends up in landfills or is shipped abroad to meet the same fate. These days I buy fewer, better-made pieces and wear them for years, as some designers now urge. My reasoning is disarmingly simple: the most sustainable garment is the one already hanging in your closet.

Imagine being offered a bet on a coin toss: if it lands heads, you win $110; if it lands tails, you lose $100. Although the wager is in your favor on average, most people decline it. Psychologists call this tendency loss aversion: the sting of losing a sum of money is felt more acutely than the pleasure of gaining the same amount. The bias helps explain why investors cling to plummeting stocks far too long, loath to admit a loss, and why shoppers react more vehemently to a surcharge than to an equivalent discount. Marketers who grasp this asymmetry often frame their offers in terms of what customers stand to lose rather than what they might gain. Hence 'Don't miss out' so often outperforms 'Get a bonus.'

Octopuses are among the most intelligent invertebrates. In laboratories they solve puzzles, unscrew the lids of jars, and occasionally escape from their tanks at night with no keeper watching. Unlike humans, they carry most of their neurons in their arms rather than in a central brain, so each arm can touch, taste, and react with a surprising degree of autonomy. Octopuses can also alter the color and texture of their skin in a fraction of a second to blend into their surroundings, yet most species are paradoxically thought to be color-blind; how they match hues they apparently cannot see remains an enigma. Their abilities are all the more striking given their brief lives: most species live only one or two years.

The sociologist Robert Merton observed that eminent scientists tend to receive disproportionate credit for a discovery compared with lesser-known researchers who make a similar contribution. When two scientists independently publish comparable findings, the more famous one is cited more often, and readers of a paper with several authors tend to remember the most prominent name. Merton called this pattern the Matthew effect, after a passage in the Gospel of Matthew about how those who have receive still more. The effect is self-reinforcing because recognition brings funding, students, and attention, and these make further recognition more likely. It can also dishearten young researchers, whose work may be overlooked simply because their names are unfamiliar to editors and readers.

For most of the digital age, lawmakers treated software as something to be regulated only after it had caused harm. The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence has unsettled that habit. In 2024 the European Union adopted a sweeping law that sorts AI systems according to the risk they pose. Applications judged to carry an unacceptable risk, such as government "social scoring" of citizens, are prohibited outright; those used in sensitive areas such as hiring, credit, and policing must meet stringent standards of transparency and human oversight; and the vast majority, from spam filters to video-game characters, face few obligations at all.
Supporters regard this graduated approach as a judicious compromise. Rather than smothering an entire technology, it concentrates scrutiny where the stakes for individuals are highest, much as societies already regulate medicines more strictly than breakfast cereals. Critics on one side contend that the rules are too lax, leaving powerful general-purpose models largely to police themselves. Critics on the other side warn that the cost of compliance will fall hardest on small start-ups without legions of lawyers and may ____ the very innovation that Europe hopes to foster.
Other governments have watched closely, and some have preferred voluntary guidelines, fearing that binding rules would drive investment elsewhere; others have begun drafting laws of their own. As AI products cross borders effortlessly, a company that wishes to sell in Europe may find it simpler to adopt European standards everywhere than to maintain separate versions for each market. Then the law could <u>punch above its weight</u>, shaping the technology far beyond the continent where it was written.

In 2025 the United States raised import duties on a scale not seen in nearly a century, and trading partners from Canada to China retaliated swiftly with measures of their own. Proponents advanced several arguments for the new tariffs. The tariffs would revive domestic manufacturing, curtail dependence on rival powers for critical goods, and give negotiators leverage to extract concessions from other countries.
Most economists remain skeptical. The reason lies in a question that sounds deceptively simple: who actually pays? A tariff is collected from the domestic company that imports the goods, not from the foreign exporter. That company can absorb the cost, eroding its own profits; it can pressure suppliers abroad to cut their prices; or it can simply pass the cost on to its customers. Studies of earlier rounds of tariffs found that <u>the third option</u> largely prevailed, leaving the burden mainly on domestic importers and the households that buy from them. In this sense a tariff functions much like a sales tax, but one rarely shown as a separate line on a receipt.
History offers a further caution: the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 was meant to insulate American farmers and factories but provoked retaliation abroad and coincided with a collapse in world trade that exacerbated the Great Depression. Few economists blame the tariff alone for the slump, but the episode is routinely cited as a lesson in how protection can invite reprisal.
Defenders reply that comparisons with the 1930s are overdrawn, and that some loss of efficiency is a price worth paying for secure supply chains. The dispute, in short, is less about arithmetic than about what a nation chooses to value.

Does the language we speak shape the way we think? The strongest form of this idea is often associated with the linguist Benjamin Lee Whorf. It holds that language determines thought and that speakers of different languages inhabit different mental worlds, a view that few researchers today would countenance. If language truly imprisoned thought, translating between languages or grasping a concept without a word in one's own language would be impossible, yet people do both easily all the time.
A weaker version of the idea, however, has garnered considerable support. Speakers of languages that use compass directions for locations, placing a cup north of a plate rather than to its left, turn out to be remarkably adept at keeping track of their orientation even inside unfamiliar buildings. Speakers of languages with separate basic words for light blue and dark blue discern those shades slightly faster than other speakers. In such cases, language does not create an ability out of nothing, but it seems to ____ certain habits of attention, much as a daily route through a city makes some streets more familiar than others.
Even these modest findings have proved contentious. Some celebrated claims have proved difficult for other laboratories to replicate, such as the suggestion that the grammatical gender of a noun colors how speakers describe objects like bridges or keys. Skeptics also caution that cultural practices rather than language itself may account for many of the observed differences. The emerging consensus is a cautious one: language is one influence on thought among many, not its master.

My grandfather repaired watches for fifty years in a shop so narrow that two customers could not stand side by side. When I was twelve, I spent a summer there, mostly sweeping the floor and sorting minuscule screws into labeled tins. I was bored. I made sure he knew it, sighing loudly whenever he asked me to fetch something. One sweltering afternoon he handed me a pocket watch that had stopped and told me, without further instruction, to find out why. I opened the case and stared at a tangle of gears, springs, and jewels so small that my breath seemed to stir them. For an hour I found nothing, and my exasperation slowly gave way to obstinacy. Then, just as I was about to give up, I noticed a single hair caught between two wheels. I removed it with a pair of tweezers while my hands quivered slightly, and when I closed the case, the watch began to tick again.
I expected praise, perhaps even a small reward. Instead my grandfather simply nodded, as if nothing remarkable had happened, and handed me another watch from the drawer. Only years later did I understand what he had given me that afternoon. It was not a lesson about watches, which I never learned to repair, but about attention: the patience to keep looking after the obvious explanations have been exhausted. When I became a doctor, I found myself returning to that narrow shop in my mind whenever a patient's symptoms refused to make sense. Somewhere, I would tell myself, <u>there is a hair caught between the wheels</u>.

For years as a primary-school teacher, I praised my pupils for being smart, believing that such praise built confidence. Research on motivation eventually convinced me that <u>this well-meant habit</u> can backfire. In a series of experiments, children who were praised for their intelligence after solving a set of puzzles were more likely to choose easy tasks afterward, apparently to protect their image as clever. When they later faced difficult problems, they lost interest quickly and performed worse. By contrast, children who had been praised for their effort tended to choose more challenging tasks and to persevere longer in the face of difficulty.
The explanation, researchers argue, lies in what the praise teaches children about ability. Praise for intelligence implies that ability is a fixed trait that one either possesses or lacks, so failure becomes evidence of a permanent shortcoming. Praise for effort implies that ability can grow, so failure becomes a signal to try a different strategy rather than a verdict on one's worth. The lesson children absorb, in other words, concerns not just a single task but the nature of their own minds.
The idea proved immensely popular, and schools around the world adopted programs designed to instill this "growth mindset." But later studies have tempered the early enthusiasm. The size of the effects varies considerably from one setting to another, and some brief classroom interventions have produced only modest gains, particularly among students who were already doing well. Critics also note that praising effort indiscriminately, even when a child has made little progress, may ring hollow. Still the core insight remains useful: what adults choose to praise sends a quiet but persistent message about what they ____.

In 2014 the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that individuals could ask search engines to remove links to information about them that was inadequate, irrelevant, or no longer relevant. The case had been brought by a Spanish man. A search for his name still produced a newspaper notice from years earlier about the forced sale of his property to pay long-settled debts. The ruling established what has come to be called the right to be forgotten.
Supporters welcomed the decision because it answered a genuinely new problem: before the internet, old newspaper stories receded from public view as they were filed away in archives; today, a single search can bring a person's worst moment back to the surface decades later. Without some way to limit this, they argue, people could never truly move on from their mistakes.
Critics, particularly in the United States, saw the ruling as a threat to free expression. In their view it forced private companies to decide case by case what the public has a right to know, a role belonging to courts and editors, not search engines. They also warned that the powerful could exploit the right to bury information that is embarrassing but genuinely ____ to the public, such as a politician's past business dealings.
Notably the ruling did not require the original newspaper to delete anything. The article remained available, although it became harder to find through a search for the man's name. The court thus sought to curb how easily information could be found, not its existence.

For generations home insurance has functioned as a quiet form of solidarity: many households pay modest premiums so that the few struck by fire or flood can rebuild, an arrangement that depends on disasters being rare and roughly predictable. As a warming climate makes wildfires, hurricanes, and floods both more frequent and more destructive, the arithmetic is beginning to falter.
In parts of the United States, the strain is already palpable. Several large insurers have stopped writing new homeowners' policies in California, citing wildfire risk and spiraling construction costs, and several smaller companies in Florida have collapsed or withdrawn after costly hurricane seasons. Wildfires swept through Los Angeles in January 2025 and destroyed thousands of homes, deepening fears that some neighborhoods may become effectively uninsurable.
Where private insurers retreat, state-backed programs often step in as insurers of last resort, typically offering more limited coverage. Such programs keep mortgages flowing, but critics argue that they merely <u>paper over the cracks</u>: by keeping premiums below the true level of risk, they encourage people to keep building and buying in places that are becoming ever more dangerous.
Economists note that rising premiums, however painful, convey valuable information. A price that reflects risk tells homeowners, builders, and local governments where it is imprudent to build new homes, and it also rewards investments in fire-resistant materials or flood defenses. The difficulty is that the households facing the steepest increases are often those least able to move. Adapting to a hotter world will require deciding not only how to share the costs of disaster but who should ultimately bear them.

When photography was introduced in 1839, some painters predicted the end of their art because a machine could now record a face or a landscape with a precision no brush could rival. What need would there be for portrait painters? For many artists who earned a living painting miniature portraits, the fear proved justified, as cheap photographic portraits rapidly took over their market. Within a few decades the miniature, once a fashionable keepsake among the well-to-do, had all but vanished.
Yet photography also liberated painting in ways few anticipated. Relieved of the duty to record appearances faithfully, painters began to probe what a camera could not capture: the play of light at a particular moment, the emotional charge of color, the inner experience of seeing. Painting with visible brushstrokes and often leaving their canvases looking unfinished, the Impressionists were in part responding to a world in which exact reproduction had become ____. Some painters even borrowed from photography itself by adopting the unorthodox cropping and frozen motion of snapshots, so that the new medium served as a source of ideas as well as a rival.
The relationship, in other words, was not simply one of replacement. A new technology took over one function of an old art form, and in doing so it pushed that older art form toward possibilities that it had barely explored before. The pattern has recurred since: the cinema did not abolish the theater, and recorded music did not silence live performance, but each forced the older form to rethink its unique offerings.

South Korea has become the starkest example of a demographic shift now spreading across wealthy nations. The total fertility rate is the average number of children a woman is expected to have over her lifetime. South Korea's rate fell to 0.72 in 2023, roughly a third of the 2.1 needed to keep a population stable without immigration. A slight rebound to 0.75 the following year was greeted with relief, but few demographers regard it as the start of a durable reversal.
Successive governments have spent lavishly on the problem, offering cash payments at birth, monthly child allowances, and subsidized childcare. Measured against the scale of the decline, the results have been <u>a drop in the bucket</u>. Surveys suggest why: young adults cite the cost of housing, cutthroat competition over education, and long working hours far more often than a shortage of public money as reasons for delaying or forgoing children. Women in particular describe a harsh ____ between career and motherhood. Taking leave can stall a promotion for years, and household duties remain unevenly shared.
The consequences extend well beyond the maternity ward, since a shrinking workforce must support a burgeoning population of retirees, straining pension funds and health systems. Rural schools are closing for lack of pupils. The armed forces face a dwindling pool of conscripts.
Few societies have managed to raise birth rates substantially. Some analysts therefore argue that the goal should shift to adapting to a smaller population through automation, later retirement, and immigration. Others insist on tackling the underlying impediments, from housing to workplace culture, for their own sake.

Despite its name, the Bayeux Tapestry is not a tapestry. A true tapestry has its design Ⓐ<u>woven</u> into the fabric on a loom, whereas the famous work in Normandy is an embroidery stitched in colored wool onto long strips of linen. Roughly seventy meters long, it narrates the Norman conquest of England in 1066, culminating at Hastings. Its scenes are remarkably Ⓑ<u>vivid</u>: soldiers tumble from horses, ships are laden with weapons and wine, and a comet blazes ominously overhead. Historians prize it as a Ⓒ<u>rare</u> visual record of eleventh-century life. Yet they also treat it with Ⓓ<u>caution</u>, because it was almost certainly made for the victors and tells the story from their perspective. Like many official histories, it is as Ⓔ<u>impartial</u> as it is beautiful, a work of persuasion disguised as a chronicle.

Why do people sometimes fail to help in an emergency when many others are present? In classic experiments in the late 1960s, John Darley and Bibb Latané found that the presence of other bystanders Ⓐ<u>reduced</u> the likelihood that any one person would intervene. Part of the reason is that people look to others to Ⓑ<u>construe</u> an ambiguous situation, and if everyone appears calm, each Ⓒ<u>infers</u> that nothing is wrong. In one study, participants completing questionnaires in a room slowly filling with smoke were far more likely to report it when alone than when seated with others who remained Ⓓ<u>alarmed</u>. Responsibility is also diffused: when many could act, each feels less obliged to do so. Awareness may help. Singling out one person in a crowd and asking directly for help can Ⓔ<u>overcome</u> the paralysis.

Twice a day, along most coasts, the sea creeps up the shore and recedes. The chief cause is the Moon's gravity, which pulls Ⓐ<u>more</u> strongly on the side of the Earth facing it than on the far side. This difference stretches the oceans into two bulges, one facing the Moon and one on the far side, and the rotating Earth carries coastlines through both. The Sun exerts a similar but Ⓑ<u>weaker</u> influence, because it is far more distant, despite its vastly greater mass. At new and full moon the Sun and Moon line up, and their effects Ⓒ<u>combine</u> to produce especially high and low tides, known as spring tides. During the quarter moons they pull at right angles, so their effects partly Ⓓ<u>reinforce</u> each other and the tidal range dwindles. Local geography can Ⓔ<u>amplify</u> these patterns dramatically.

Why do I cherish the wobbly bookshelf I assembled myself more than the sturdier one I bought ready-made? Psychologists have a name for this tendency: the IKEA effect, after the furniture retailer whose products arrive flat-packed and require assembly. In a series of studies, participants who built simple storage boxes or folded origami figures valued their creations considerably more than identical items made by others, and they presumed that other people would share their enthusiasm. But the effect depended on completion: when participants built something and then dismantled it, or left it unfinished, the extra attachment largely dissipated. The finding suggests that labor does not merely produce objects. It also produces affection for them, at least when the effort ends in success. Designers who ask customers to contribute a little work may therefore be selling more than a product.

In the 1920s and early 1930s researchers at the Hawthorne Works, a large electrical factory near Chicago, set out to discover how working conditions affected productivity. In one famous series of tests, they raised and lowered the lighting in a workroom. To their puzzlement, output seemed to improve almost regardless of the changes, even in dimmer light by some accounts. One prevailing interpretation held that the workers were responding not to the lighting but to the attention: knowing they were being studied, they worked harder. This idea, later dubbed the Hawthorne effect, entered textbooks as a caveat that observation itself can alter behavior. But scholars who later reexamined the surviving data found the original evidence far weaker and murkier than the legend suggests, a reminder that even celebrated findings warrant a second look.

Tardigrades, often called water bears, are microscopic animals that rarely grow longer than about a millimeter. Magnified, they resemble plump, eight-legged caterpillars lumbering through films of water on moss. Their renown rests on an extraordinary capacity to survive conditions lethal to almost any other animal. In dry surroundings many species expel nearly all the water from their bodies, curl into a shriveled state known as a tun, and suspend their metabolism almost entirely. In this condition they can endure extreme cold, intense radiation, and, in one experiment, even exposure to the vacuum of outer space, reviving when water returns. But tardigrades are not invincible in their active state. Outside the tun, they are as vulnerable as other tiny creatures. Their resilience is a strategy for waiting out bad times, not for thriving in them.

Why do songs that irritated me on first hearing so often become my favorites after a few weeks on the radio? In the late 1960s the psychologist Robert Zajonc reported a series of experiments suggesting an answer. Participants were shown unfamiliar stimuli, such as nonsense words or Chinese characters they could not read, some of them many times and others only once or twice. When later asked to rate how much they liked each item, they consistently preferred the ones they had seen more often even though they could not say what the items meant, a pattern Zajonc called the mere exposure effect. Familiarity apparently breeds not contempt but a modest fondness, perhaps because the familiar feels safe. The effect has limits, however: repeating something people already dislike can deepen their aversion, and endless repetition eventually breeds tedium.

Commentators dubbed 2024 the biggest election year in history: countries with roughly half of the world's population held national votes, from India and Indonesia to Mexico, the United Kingdom, and the United States. It was also the first such year in which persuasive fake audio and video could be produced cheaply by almost anyone with a laptop. Early in the year an automated telephone message imitating the voice of the American president exhorted voters in New Hampshire to skip a primary election, and fabricated clips of candidates circulated in several other countries.
Many observers braced for chaos, but in the event, a number of post-election reviews concluded that deepfakes had done less to sway results than feared. Most fabricated clips were quickly debunked, and those that spread widely tended to reach partisans whose minds were already made up. But researchers cautioned that this relative calm should not be mistaken for safety. A single well-timed forgery released hours before polls open may leave no time for ____.
Moreover the greatest damage may be indirect. Once the public knows that any recording can be forged, politicians caught on tape saying something embarrassing gain a convenient alibi: they can simply claim that the evidence is fake, a tactic legal scholars call <u>the liar's dividend</u>. Its corrosive effect does not depend on any particular forgery succeeding. It depends only on a pervasive atmosphere of doubt. Some experts therefore argue that technical fixes such as labeling machine-generated content must be accompanied by efforts to bolster trusted sources of news. Citizens will then still have somewhere to turn when they can no longer believe their own eyes.

Across the developed world, people are living longer and having fewer children, and the arithmetic of retirement is shifting accordingly. Under many pension systems as first designed, a worker retiring at sixty could expect to draw benefits for a decade or so. Today that period often stretches beyond twenty years, and the number of workers contributing for each retiree inexorably declines. One expedient, increasingly favored by governments, is to keep people working longer. France raised its minimum pension age from 62 to 64 in 2023 despite months of protests, a change later mired in political wrangling. In South Korea the legal retirement age is sixty, and a debate over extending it to sixty-five has intensified.
Advocates point out that today's sixty-year-olds are on average healthier and better educated than any previous generation of that age and that many of them want or need to keep earning. Retaining seasoned employees on the payroll, they add, can alleviate labor shortages and safeguard skills that take decades to acquire.
Detractors raise two objections, the first concerning fairness between occupations: a lawyer may welcome a few extra years at her desk, but a construction worker whose body is worn out by fifty-five may experience <u>the same reform</u> as a cut in benefits rather than an opportunity. The second concerns fairness between generations. In firms where pay rises automatically with seniority, older employees are costly to retain, and young job seekers fear that extending older workers' tenure will ____ the number of openings available to new graduates.
Many economists therefore argue that raising the retirement age works best when combined with other changes, such as pay based on role rather than years of service and arrangements allowing gradual rather than abrupt retirement.

Generative AI systems learn to write and draw by analyzing enormous quantities of text and images, much of it copied from the open web without the permission of those who created it. For several years this practice attracted scant legal scrutiny, but that changed as the systems became commercially lucrative. Since 2023 novelists, illustrators, photo agencies, music publishers, and a major American newspaper have filed lawsuits against AI developers, arguing that copying their work to build a competing product amounts to infringement on an industrial scale.
The developers' defense rests largely on the American doctrine of fair use, which permits certain unlicensed uses of copyrighted material if the new use is transformative rather than a mere substitute for the original. A model, they argue, does not store and resell books or pictures. It extracts statistical patterns from them, much as a human student assimilates a style by reading widely. Creators retort that the analogy is ____. A student cannot read millions of books in a month, and a student's essays do not inundate the market that sustains the student's teachers.
Early rulings have pointed in divergent directions. Some judges have treated training as transformative but stressed that illegally obtained copies or outputs reproducing protected passages nearly word for word may still expose companies to liability. Meanwhile many developers have begun signing licensing deals with publishers and image libraries, a sign that they regard paying for data as cheaper than prolonged litigation. Whatever the courts finally decide, the disputes have forced an old question into a new form: when a machine learns from human work, what, if anything, does it owe the people who made it?

Heat is often called a silent killer, and nowhere is it quieter than on a construction site or a farm. Unlike floods, a heat wave leaves no visible wreckage, yet it can be just as lethal for people who must keep working through it. As 2024 became the hottest year on record worldwide, protecting outdoor workers moved toward the center of labor policy.
When the air is both hot and humid, sweat evaporates sluggishly and the body's internal temperature climbs. Early symptoms such as dizziness are easily dismissed by laborers paid by the piece or anxious about forfeiting a day's wages, and by the time collapse occurs it may be too late. Several governments now mandate rest breaks in the shade once temperatures pass a certain threshold. But enforcement is another matter. Inspectors are scarce, and on a site racing to meet a deadline a compulsory break can quietly <u>fall by the wayside</u>.

The summer I turned nineteen, I set out to travel alone through the mountains of a country whose language I could barely read. On the fourth day I misread a timetable and arrived at a village bus stop twenty minutes after the last bus of the evening had departed. The road was empty, the light was fading, and my phone was dead because I had forgotten to charge it. I remember checking the timetable again and again, as if the numbers might rearrange themselves in my favor, while my heart pounded and every rustle in the trees sounded ominous.
A light was still on in a tiny shop across the road. The elderly woman inside scrutinized my face, my backpack, and the useless timetable in my hand and seemed to grasp my predicament without a word. She sat me down beside a kerosene heater, poured me a bowl of barley tea, and made a telephone call. Half an hour later her nephew arrived in a battered truck and drove me to the nearest town, declining the money I tried to press into his hand. By the time I reached my guesthouse the panic had drained out of me, leaving only a warm and slightly dazed gratitude.
I never learned the woman's name, and I could not find the village again on any map. Perhaps that is why the evening has stayed with me. A kindness that cannot be repaid to the giver has to go somewhere else, so for twenty years now I have been <u>settling the account with strangers</u>: giving directions, lending a charger, waiting with someone at a station until their ride appears.

In 1912 a German meteorologist named Alfred Wegener proposed an idea that most geologists of his day regarded as little short of absurd: the continents had once been joined in a single landmass and had slowly drifted apart over millions of years.
(A) The objection that proved decisive was not about his evidence but about his explanation. Wegener could not offer a cogent account of what force might push entire continents through the solid rock of the ocean floor, and the mechanisms he posited were shown to be woefully inadequate. Without a mechanism, critics concluded, drift was ____, a story that fit the facts too neatly to be trusted. By the time Wegener died on an expedition to Greenland in 1930, his theory had few defenders.
(B) The vindication came from a place Wegener could never have examined. After the Second World War, surveys of the ocean floor revealed a vast underwater mountain chain running down the middle of the Atlantic and symmetrical stripes of magnetized rock on either side of it. New crust was continually forming at such ridges and spreading outward, carrying the continents with it. By the late 1960s, the theory of plate tectonics had absorbed Wegener's central claim, and drift became textbook orthodoxy.
(C) His evidence was varied and, in hindsight, compelling: the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like pieces of a puzzle. Fossils of the same ancient plants and reptiles turned up on continents now separated by thousands of kilometers of ocean, creatures that could hardly have swum across. Rock formations and the traces of ancient glaciers likewise appeared to match on opposite sides of the Atlantic.

When Samuel Johnson published his Dictionary of the English Language in 1755, many readers hoped it would do for English what academies in France and Italy had attempted for their own languages: fix it in a correct and permanent form. Johnson had begun the project with similar ambitions, but by the time he finished roughly nine years later he had largely forsaken them. In his preface he conceded that no dictionary could stop a living language from changing, for words shift along with the habits of the people who use them.
That admission foreshadowed a profound metamorphosis in how dictionaries are made. In the following century, the editors of what became the Oxford English Dictionary set out not to legislate usage but to record it. They enlisted hundreds of volunteer readers, who combed through books of every period and mailed in slips of paper showing each word in context. Among the most prolific contributors was a surgeon confined to an asylum, who supplied many thousands of quotations. The editors then traced how meanings had emerged, multiplied, and faded over time. The undertaking was so vast that the first complete edition did not appear until 1928, decades after work had begun.
This descriptive approach did not end the quarrel. It merely relocated it. When an American dictionary published in 1961 included informal and nonstandard words with few warnings about their status, critics accused its editors of abandoning standards altogether and newspapers lamented what they saw as a capitulation to sloppiness. Defenders retorted that a dictionary which ignores how millions of people actually speak is not guarding the language but misrepresenting it.
The dispute persists because <u>both camps</u> are partly right. Speakers do want guidance, especially in formal writing, and a dictionary that offers none leaves them adrift. Yet guidance that pretends usage never moves soon becomes obsolete. Modern lexicographers have settled on an uneasy compromise, describing usage faithfully while adding labels that flag words likely to raise eyebrows in a job application.

In the 1790s the Italian scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani noticed something perplexing about bats. Blindfolded bats, and even bats whose eyes had been removed, could still fly through a darkened room strung with threads without colliding with them. Yet when their ears were plugged, they blundered helplessly into obstacles. Spallanzani concluded that bats somehow saw with their ears, but he could not explain how, and many contemporaries dismissed the idea as fanciful. The answer had to wait until the late 1930s, when the American researcher Donald Griffin used equipment able to detect sounds above the range of human hearing. He showed that bats emit rapid, high-pitched calls and listen for the echoes, a process he called echolocation.
By analyzing the returning echoes, a hunting bat can judge not only the distance to an insect but also its size, direction, and even the beating of its wings. As the bat closes in, its calls become faster and culminate in a rapid burst just before capture, which gives it continually updated information about its quarry.
But prey have not remained ____. Many moths have evolved ears attuned to bat calls, and when they detect an approaching bat they dive, loop, or drop toward the ground. Some tiger moths go further, producing ultrasonic clicks of their own that may startle bats, warn them that the moth tastes foul, or even jam their sonar. The result is an evolutionary arms race conducted entirely in sounds that humans cannot hear.
Remarkably, some blind people have taught themselves a version of the same skill, producing sharp tongue clicks and interpreting the faint echoes to sense the shape and position of nearby objects.

Before the age of the railway, time was a local affair. Each town set its clocks by the sun, declaring noon at the moment the sun stood highest overhead. Because the sun reaches that point a little later as one travels west, a town's clocks might differ by several minutes from those of a neighbor only a short distance away. For people who traveled no faster than a horse, the discrepancy hardly mattered.
The railways changed that, for a train covering hundreds of kilometers in a day passed through dozens of local times, and timetables that tried to accommodate them all became nearly unintelligible. Worse, confusion about the time on a single-track line could send two trains toward each other. British railway companies began adopting a single standard based on Greenwich in the 1840s, and in 1883 the railroads of the United States and Canada replaced a bewildering patchwork of local times with a handful of time zones. The following year, an international conference in Washington chose the meridian passing through Greenwich as the reference point for the world's longitude.
Not everyone welcomed the change: some communities resented having their clocks dictated by distant companies, and for a time a number of towns obstinately kept local time alongside the new standard. Critics grumbled that <u>railway time</u> served the convenience of commerce rather than the rhythms of nature. Yet within a generation, the standardized hour had become so ____ that few people could imagine life without it. Today our phones quietly synchronize themselves with atomic clocks, and it is easy to forget that the time we take for granted was once a deliberate and contested invention.

In April 1815 Mount Tambora on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa erupted in the most powerful volcanic explosion in recorded history. The blast killed tens of thousands of people nearby, but its effects reached much farther. Enormous quantities of sulfur gas rose into the upper atmosphere, where they formed a haze that Ⓐ<u>reflected</u> sunlight back into space. The following year, 1816, became known in Europe and North America as the Year Without a Summer. Snow fell in New England in June, harvests Ⓑ<u>failed</u> across much of Europe, and food prices soared. Unaware of any link between volcanoes and climate, people at the time found the strange weather Ⓒ<u>baffling</u>. Today scientists regard the episode as a Ⓓ<u>trivial</u> illustration of how a single eruption can disrupt the global climate, a lesson they consider Ⓔ<u>relevant</u> to modern proposals to cool the planet artificially.

In college I took lecture notes on a laptop because I could type far Ⓐ<u>faster</u> than I could write, yet speed may not be an Ⓑ<u>advantage</u>. In several studies, students who typed could keep Ⓒ<u>pace</u> with the lecturer and reproduce what was said nearly word for word. In other words, they tended to Ⓓ<u>summarize</u> lectures rather than think about them. Those writing by hand could not keep up and were forced to condense what they heard into their own words, and this effort of selection and rephrasing appears to Ⓔ<u>deepen</u> understanding. When tested on the concepts later, hand-writers often performed as well as or better than typists. Later research has been mixed, but the findings suggest that the most efficient method of recording information is not always the most effective way of learning it.

Coral reefs owe their brilliant colors largely to microscopic algae that live inside the tissues of coral animals. The partnership is Ⓐ<u>mutually</u> beneficial: the algae receive shelter, and in return they supply the coral with most of the food it needs through photosynthesis. When ocean temperatures rise even a degree or two above normal for several weeks, however, this relationship breaks down. Stressed corals Ⓑ<u>expel</u> their algae, exposing their white skeletons, a process known as bleaching. Bleached corals are not yet dead, and if the water cools quickly they can Ⓒ<u>recover</u>. But prolonged heat leaves them Ⓓ<u>starving</u> and vulnerable to disease. As marine heat waves have grown more frequent, scientists worry that reefs are being given ever less time to recuperate between episodes, rendering their long-term survival increasingly Ⓔ<u>assured</u>.

Scientific journals have long preferred to publish studies with striking, positive results: a drug that works, an effect that appears. By contrast, studies that find nothing are often rejected or never submitted at all, consigned to what researchers ruefully call the file drawer. The habit seems innocuous, yet it systematically distorts the scientific record. If twenty teams test an ineffective treatment, one may obtain a positive result by sheer chance. If only that study is published, the treatment will appear to work. To counter this bias, some journals now agree to publish a study on the basis of its design before the results are known, and many funders require that clinical trials be registered in advance. A null result can be as informative as a discovery, provided anyone is allowed to see it.

For centuries Egyptian hieroglyphs were a closed book. Scholars assumed that the elaborate symbols were purely pictorial, each one standing for an idea rather than a sound, and their attempts at translation produced little more than fanciful guesses. The breakthrough came from a slab of stone discovered by French soldiers in 1799 near the town of Rosetta. It bore the same decree in three scripts: hieroglyphic, a later Egyptian script known as demotic, and ancient Greek, already readable to scholars. By painstakingly comparing the texts, the French scholar Jean-François Champollion demonstrated in 1822 that hieroglyphs combined phonetic signs with symbols for whole words. His insight opened up three thousand years of Egyptian history and allowed the ancient Egyptians to speak in their own words after more than a millennium of silence.

The axolotl, a salamander native to a handful of lakes and canals near Mexico City, is famous for an unusual trait: it never fully grows up. Most amphibians lose their gills and move onto land as they mature, but the axolotl typically retains its feathery external gills and spends its entire life in water, a condition biologists call neoteny. It is also a prodigy of regeneration, able to regrow lost limbs, parts of its spinal cord, and even portions of its heart without scarring. These abilities have made it a favorite of laboratory researchers investigating how tissues repair themselves. Ironically, countless axolotls thrive in laboratories and home aquariums around the world while the wild species has become critically endangered through pollution and urban expansion as well as introduced fish.

In 1999 the psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger published a study suggesting that people who perform poorly on tests of logic, grammar, and humor tend to overestimate their abilities dramatically. Those who scored near the bottom often rated themselves above average. The researchers proposed that the least competent are <u>doubly handicapped</u>: the skills required to perform well in a domain are often the very skills required to recognize good performance, so such people not only err but also fail to perceive their own shortcomings. Intriguingly, top performers showed the opposite tendency and slightly underestimated their standing, apparently because they assumed that tasks easy for them were equally easy for everyone. Some statisticians have since called part of the pattern a statistical artifact, but the finding remains widely cited.

For decades cities competed fiercely for tourists, treating every additional visitor as a welcome boost to local prosperity, but in many destinations that consensus is fraying. Residents of popular old towns lament that short-term rentals have driven up rents and hollowed out neighborhoods. Bakeries and hardware stores have given way to souvenir shops, and narrow streets become nearly impassable in peak season. In the summer of 2024 demonstrators in Barcelona marched through tourist districts, and some squirted visitors with water pistols to dramatize their exasperation.
Authorities have begun to experiment with ways of taming the crowds. In 2024 Venice became the first major city to charge day-trippers an entry fee, initially five euros on the busiest days. Japan introduced a fee and a daily cap for climbers on the most popular trail up Mount Fuji. Elsewhere cities have curbed new holiday rentals, restricted large tour groups, or raised levies on overnight stays. The rationale is straightforward: when visitors impose costs on residents beyond the price of a trip, a charge can make them ____ part of this burden.
Skeptics doubt that such measures will accomplish much, for a fee of a few euros is negligible compared with the cost of flights and hotels, and few economists expect so modest a charge to deter many visitors. Some suspect that officials are merely dressing up a revenue grab as crowd control. Others worry that steep charges could turn historic centers into playgrounds reserved for the affluent.
Still, the debate marks a notable shift, as tourism is increasingly regarded not as an unalloyed blessing but as a resource like water or road space, to be rationed when demand outstrips supply.

Beneath the floor of a forest lies a network that few visitors ever contemplate. The roots of most trees are colonized by fungi whose threadlike filaments ramify through the soil, absorbing water and minerals for the trees in exchange for sugars. A single fungus can attach to the roots of several trees at once, so scientists realized that trees might be linked through these subterranean threads in a web that journalists soon nicknamed the wood wide web.
The idea captivated the public imagination, and popular books and documentaries portrayed forests as cooperative communities in which venerable mother trees nourish their seedlings, send carbon to struggling neighbors, and warn one another of insect attacks through chemical signals traveling along the fungal network. Forests, in this telling, were less an aggregate of competing individuals than a kind of society.
In recent years, however, a number of researchers have urged caution. Reviewing the field in 2023, a group of ecologists argued that the evidence for some of the most popular claims is far thinner than public enthusiasm suggests. They acknowledged that shared networks clearly exist. But experiments showing meaningful transfers of resources between trees, with real benefits to the receiving tree, are scarce and often amenable to other interpretations. Many studies, they noted, had been cited in ways that went well beyond what their authors had found.
None of this means that the underground world is unimportant. Fungi are indispensable to the health of forests. The lesson, the skeptics suggest, is that a vivid story can ____ the data on which it rests and that scientists must take care not to let a seductive metaphor supplant evidence.

Short-form video has become the lingua franca of the smartphone. Platforms built around clips lasting seconds rather than minutes now attract well over a billion users, and older services have hurried to emulate the format. Their allure is not hard to fathom: each swipe offers something new, and recommendation algorithms learn with uncanny speed which clips will keep a particular viewer watching.
Critics worry that <u>this endless novelty</u> exacts a price. The next reward is always a flick of the thumb away, so heavy users may grow impatient with anything that demands sustained effort, from a long novel to an intricate lecture. As a teacher I watch students struggle to sit through a full-length film without reaching for their phones, and I confess to finding it harder to immerse myself in a book than I once did.
But the scientific evidence is less conclusive than the anecdotes. Studies have found correlations between heavy short-video use and weaker self-reported attention, but most are surveys taken at a single point in time, which cannot establish what causes what. People who already find concentration arduous may simply gravitate toward rapid, easily digested content. Researchers also note that the shrinking attention span has been blamed in turn on television, video games, and the early internet.
What seems clearer is that attention behaves less like a fixed capacity than like a habit. Tasks we practice become easier, while those we shun grow more daunting. A reader who fills every idle moment with scrolling is not necessarily losing the ability to focus, but may be ____ it, much as an unused muscle atrophies without disappearing.

"Every page," Mrs. Okafor said, tapping the lid of a cardboard box. "We read every page before anything goes." She was a retired seamstress from two doors down, and my mother had arranged for me to help her sort through her late husband's study during my school vacation. I agreed only for the promised pay and arrived on the first morning determined to finish as expeditiously as possible. The room was crammed with boxes of letters, receipts, and notebooks, and she meant exactly what she had said. By the third day I was openly sulking, sighing theatrically whenever she lingered over a faded envelope.
On the fourth afternoon she handed me a notebook and asked me to read it aloud, since her eyes tired easily. It turned out to be a diary her husband had kept during his first year in this country, when he worked nights in a bakery and slept in a rented room he shared with two strangers. He wrote about the cold, about money, about missing his mother's voice. Then, on a page dated in early spring, he described meeting a young woman at a bus stop who had laughed at his dreadful joke. Mrs. Okafor said nothing, but when I looked up she was smiling with her eyes closed.
I did not sulk again that summer. I began to understand that we were not clearing out a room but <u>listening to a life</u>, and that the slowness I had resented was a form of reverence. She later gave me the diary's last page, which still hangs in a frame above my desk.

The electric car is often marketed as a clean machine, but every one of them depends on a long and frequently grimy supply chain. Its battery requires lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, and other minerals. These must be extracted, refined, and assembled into cells before a single vehicle leaves the factory. As sales of electric vehicles have climbed, governments have begun to regard this chain less as a matter of commerce than as one of national security.
The anxiety stems from concentration: a large share of the world's cobalt is mined in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, often under conditions criticized trenchantly by human-rights groups. China dominates the refining of many battery minerals and the manufacture of the cells themselves. Countries hoping to build battery industries of their own therefore find themselves dependent on a ____ that is also a strategic rival. In ordinary times such reliance may seem a reasonable bargain, since Chinese producers have invested heavily and offer low prices. In a crisis, critics warn, it could prove a crippling vulnerability.
In response the United States, the European Union, and others have offered generous subsidies to encourage mining, refining, and battery production at home or among trusted partners. Skeptics note that these policies can raise costs for consumers and provoke disputes with trading partners and that new mines and refineries take many years to build amid fierce local opposition over pollution and water use. A mine approved today may not yield ore until the next decade.
Engineers, meanwhile, are attacking the problem from another direction. Batteries based on lithium iron phosphate require no cobalt or nickel and have rapidly gained market share, and researchers are developing sodium-ion cells that dispense with lithium altogether. Recycling may eventually supply a meaningful fraction of the minerals needed, as the first generation of electric cars reaches the scrapyard. None of these innovations will end the scramble for raw materials soon, but together they suggest that the map of dependence is not immutable.

Every flat map of the world is a compromise. It is impossible to peel the curved surface of a globe and press it flat without stretching or tearing it somewhere, so mapmakers must decide which properties to preserve and which to sacrifice. No projection is neutral. Each embodies a judgment about what matters most.
In 1569 the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator published a map designed with sailors in mind. Its great virtue was that a line of constant compass bearing appeared on it as a straight line, so a navigator could draw a course between two ports with a ruler and then simply hold a single heading. For long ocean voyages, this made the map an extraordinarily practical tool, and it gradually became the standard chart of European seafarers.
The price of this convenience was a conspicuous distortion of size. To keep angles true, the projection must stretch regions more and more as they approach the poles. Greenland appears roughly as large as Africa, although Africa is in fact about fourteen times larger, and Europe looks far bigger relative to the equatorial world than it really is.
These distortions mattered little at sea, but the map soon left the navigator's cabin. Reproduced in atlases and hung on classroom walls for generations, it shaped how millions of people pictured the planet, and critics later argued that it subtly inflated the importance of Europe and North America. Many educators now prefer compromise projections for world maps, yet a version of the old design survives in online street maps, where preserving the shapes of small areas remains paramount.

In a widely cited experiment published in 2000, researchers set up a tasting table in an upscale California grocery store that displayed either six varieties of jam or twenty-four. The larger display attracted more visitors, yet shoppers who saw only six flavors were far more likely to actually buy a jar. The study helped popularize the notion of choice overload: beyond a certain point, adding options does not liberate consumers but <u>leaves them paralyzed</u>, fretful about choosing wrongly and less satisfied with whatever they finally select.
The idea resonated because it contradicted a cherished tenet of economics: more choice can never make a rational person worse off, for one can always ignore the superfluous options. Retailers pruned their product lines, and advisers suggested that retirement plans offer fewer funds.
But later research complicated the picture. Psychologists pooled the results of dozens of studies and found the average effect of large assortments to be close to zero: in some experiments abundant choice discouraged decisions, but in others it had no effect or even helped. The crucial question, it seems, is not how many options are offered but under what conditions. Choice overload appears most likely when people lack clear preferences, when the options are hard to compare, and when the decision must be made in haste.
For designers of menus, websites, and public programs the practical lesson is therefore not simply to slash the number of options but to make them easier to navigate. Sorting products into clear categories, highlighting a sensible default, and elucidating the differences that genuinely matter can let people relish variety without being overwhelmed by it.

For decades physicists have quipped that a working fusion reactor is perpetually three decades off. Fusion powers the sun and releases prodigious amounts of energy when light atomic nuclei are forced together. On Earth it requires heating fuel to many millions of degrees and confining it long enough for reactions to occur. The task is so formidable that no experiment had ever produced more energy from its fuel than was delivered to it.
That changed in December 2022. Scientists at a national laboratory in California fired powerful lasers at a tiny fuel capsule and for the first time obtained more fusion energy than the lasers had deposited in the target. The feat was hailed as historic but came with <u>an important asterisk</u>: the facility as a whole consumed far more electricity to power its lasers than the reaction released, so the experiment was a scientific milestone rather than a practical source of power.
Since then enthusiasm has spread beyond government laboratories. Private fusion companies have raised billions of dollars, and some technology firms anxious about the voracious electricity demands of their data centers have signed agreements to buy power from fusion plants that do not yet exist. Meanwhile the international ITER project in southern France, intended to demonstrate fusion on an industrial scale, has suffered repeated delays and cost overruns.
Skeptics point out that daunting engineering obstacles remain, from materials that can withstand relentless bombardment by neutrons to the challenge of producing fuel. Even optimists concede that fusion is unlikely to contribute much to curbing emissions in the coming decade, the very period of greatest urgency for the transition away from fossil fuels. Wind, solar power, and batteries, already cheap and proven, must shoulder this burden.

An ancient puzzle recorded by Plutarch concerns the ship of Theseus, which the Athenians preserved for centuries by replacing each decaying plank with a new one. Once every original plank was gone, was it still the same ship? And if someone had gathered the discarded planks and reassembled them, which vessel would have the stronger claim? The riddle bears on questions we care about deeply, for our cells are continually renewed and our convictions shift over the years. It also has practical stakes, for courts must decide whether an offender convicted decades later is truly the person who committed the crime, and conservators must judge how much of an old building can be renewed before it becomes a mere replica of itself. Perhaps the deepest lesson of the puzzle is that identity is less a fact waiting to be discovered than a ____ that reflects what we choose to value.

When the Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer, better known as ENIAC, was unveiled to the press in 1946, newspapers marveled at a machine capable of thousands of calculations a second. Built at the University of Pennsylvania to compute artillery firing tables for the U.S. Army, it filled a large room, contained some eighteen thousand vacuum tubes, and devoured prodigious amounts of electricity. The engineers who designed its circuitry were lionized as pioneers. Far less attention went to the small team of women who had worked out how to make it do anything at all.
ENIAC could not Ⓐ<u>store</u> programs in the modern sense. To tackle a new problem, operators had to Ⓑ<u>rewire</u> it by hand, plugging cables and setting thousands of switches according to diagrams of their own design, often with little more than the machine's blueprints to guide them. The work demanded Ⓒ<u>formidable</u> mathematical skill and an intimate grasp of the hardware, since a single misplaced cable could vitiate an entire calculation. Yet at the time, programming was widely regarded as Ⓓ<u>prestigious</u> clerical work, a mere extension of the hand computation that women had long performed for the military. In publicity photographs, the women frequently went unidentified, treated as little more than <u>part of the scenery</u>.
Only decades later did historians begin to Ⓔ<u>recover</u> their story, interviewing the surviving programmers and restoring their names to the record. Their belated recognition illustrates a recurrent pattern in the history of technology: the prestige of a task often depends less on its intrinsic difficulty than on who happens to perform it. Once programming came to be seen as intellectually demanding and lucrative, it was gradually redefined as a predominantly male profession and the contributions of its earliest practitioners receded from view.
